title: The heart of the world's longest living vertebrate: the Greenland shark

authors.affiliation: Faculty of Biology, Medicine and Health, University of Manchester, UK

abstract_text: The life span of the Greenland shark is at least 272 years and may be as long as 500 years making this animal the longest living vertebrate on the planet. It was one of the lesser-known species of sharks up until 2016 when its extreme longevity was revealed. The finding that they live in the deep, dark Arctic waters for hundreds of years has captured the imagination of the world and the attention of scientists. How does an animal born in Shakespeare's time still patrol the deep today? This extreme longevity is particularly interesting with respect to the heart, because heart disease is synonymous with aging in humans. What structures do their hearts have that permit this extreme longevity? Does the heart underlie the ability of this shark to live so long? We investigated cardiac tissue from 8 sharks whose ages range between ~ 100±120 to 210 ±120 years old and found significant fibrosis, evidence of cardiomyocyte proliferation and regeneration and unusual mitochondrial biology. We did not find evidence of atherosclerosis. These findings will be discussed in relation to the idea of chronological age versus 'biological' age.

title: Nervous control of ventilation and heart rate in the brainstem of the dogfish, Scyliorhinus canicula, a neuranatomical and neurophysiological study

authors.affiliation: School of Biosciences, University of Birmingham, UK

abstract_text: Injection of neural tracers into selected branches of cranial nerves V, VII, IX and X that innervate respiratory muscles and the heart of the elasmobranch fish, Scyliorhinus canicula identified their progressive rostro-caudal distribution into discrete nuclei in the brainstem. Efferent activity recorded from nerves supplying respiratory muscles inserted on the jaws, hyomandibular and gill arches displayed sequential bursting activity, driving gill ventilation. This activity, which may be derive from a respiratory rhythm generator located in the reticular formation, was relayed via the trigeminal Vth nucleus, with subsequent activity in the VIIth, IXth and Xth nuclei reflecting their location in the brainstem. Forced ventilation is achieved by recruitment of feeding muscles, innervated by occipital and anterior spinal nerves. The heart and branchial (gill) circulation in elasmobranch fishes is innervated solely by the parasympathetic vagus nerve. Recordings from cardiac branches of the vagus showed two types of activity: units with regular, respiration-related activity and arrhythmic activity that increased during hypoxia and in response to J-recepter stimulation. Injection of neural tracers into the cardiac nerves revealed that cardiac, vagal, preganglionic neurons (CVPN) have their cell bodies in two locations in the brainstem: medial (m) within the dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus (DVN) and a ventro-lateral scattered distribution (vl) outside of the DVN. Location of these cell bodies by insertion into the brainstem of recording micro-electrodes revealed that m cells showed respiration-related activity while vl cells did not. Both cell groups responded to mechanical stimulation of gill arches. Although tonic, peripheral electrical stimulation of cardiac branches of the vagus inhibited the heart, phasic stimulation recruited the heart at rates faster or slower than its intrinsic rate. A simple model attempting to explain the nature and significance of some of these interactions has been proposed.

abstract_text: Despite their evolutionary success, many chondrichthyans are increasingly threatened with extinction as a result of human activities and the conservative life history traits of this group of fishes. In Mediterranean basin, the thornback ray (Raja clavata), represents among the Rajids the most commercially utilized species and it is actually included in the IUCN-RedList as Threatened species. In particular, in the West-Central Mediterranean basin, where the fishing activity is well-developed, R. clavata represents one of the most important by-catch species mostly for the bottom trawl and long line fishery. Despite being a very widespread species, some gaps still exist on its biology mostly on the growth pattern. The lack of biological data constitutes, for the Mediterranean, one of the impediments in order to assess and take appropriate management measures for this species. Indeed, stock-assessment models, particularly the analytical ones, require growth parameters as important input data. The aim of the present study is to fill this knowledge gap. Specimens of R. clavata were collected during the experimental trawl surveys, commercial landings and discard monitoring in Sardinia, Central-Southern Tyrrhenian, West Ionian and South Adriatic Sea. Thin sections of vertebrae were performed in order to determinate the age and calculate the von Bertalanffy growth function parameters for both sexes in each study area. Moreover, on specimens captured in Adriatic, Sardinia and West Ionian, the marginal increment analysis (MIA) of the vertebrae was also carried out as a semidirect ageing analysis validation. In the Adriatic, a mark-recapture experiment, marking by both external (spaghetti tags) and chemical (oxytetracycline injection) tags, 98 specimens of R. clavata was also realized. In total two recaptures after 11 and 14 months were recorded with an increment in total length respectively of 11.4 cm (from 49.5 to 60.9 cm) and 10.3 cm (from 63.5 to 73.8 cm). In both specimens recaptured the oxytetracycline mark together with the subsequent deposition of a completed annulus (one transparent and opaque ring) was observed on the sections of vertebrae.

abstract_text: Morphometric characters have traditionally been used to describe fish population structures and differences between populations. They have been found to be of taxonomic importance in sex, race and species identification as well. Knowledge involving the taxonomy, systematics and life history of rays and skates that inhabit the Mediterranean basin is scarce. Up to date the importance of batoids in small-scale fisheries in the Greek waters is not well-known, possibly due to the taxonomic uncertainties concerning several taxa. The aim of this work was to present for the first time the morphometric characters of Raja clavata in the eastern Ionian Sea, in order to identify differences between sexes and compare them to other rajids in future references. Intraspecific variation in the external morphology of the thornback ray was investigated and described on the basis of 35 morphometric variables, from 77 females (140-780 mm in total length) and 63 males (135-690 mm in total length). For each morphometric value the mean, standard deviation, range and coefficient variation (CV) were estimated for each sex separately. Regression models were applied to estimate the relationships between each morphometric character and total length. The pattern of allometry for each parameter was established by testing the slope (b) of the obtained regression equations against isometry applying the Student's t-test. (b = 1 for length-length or 3 for length-weight). The length-weight relationship was determined according to the following equation: W=a*TLb. Differences between sexes were tested with t-test. Further investigation on different sizes of R.clavata will contribute to the knowledge of the stock biology, physiology and ecology.

abstract_text: The body (somatic) growth of individuals is a vital process that governs many aspects of a species' life history. Thus, knowledge about growth parameters is critical in many assessment methods. Such growth parameters are derived by relating individual length to age, with the latter commonly estimated from growth bands formed in calcified structures. Recent research, however, suggests that these structures cannot be used for aging in many elasmobranchs (sharks, rays and skates). Alternative methods from mark-recapture tagging data have been proposed in the past, but have not been rigorously tested on elasmobranchs. Therefore, the performance of seven different methods in estimating von Bertalanffy growth parameters for elasmobranchs is investigated here. The performance of the methods were evaluated in two ways: 1) Estimated growth parameters from simulated datasets that considered individual growth variability, measurement error and different scenarios for the length at capture, times at liberty and sample size were compared to the true growth parameters in the simulation; 2) Growth parameters were estimated from empirical mark-recapture tagging data for 15 different elasmobranch stocks and compared to literature growth parameters obtained from length-at-age information. Best practicies when only limited information from mark-recapture tagging data is available will be presented with practical applications and common pitfalls discussed.

abstract_text: The different effects of fishing capture are not just immediate death; unwanted animals are released back into the environment to an unknown fate, as injuries and physiological, physical and behavioural consequences can ultimately lead to delayed mortality and/or impact their fitness. In teleosts, extensive research has highlighted that fisheries stress can negatively affect reproduction by impairing individuals' ability to contribute to the increase in population abundance and neonates' survival and performance. Despite being one of the most threatened aquatic taxa, data on the reproductive consequences of fishing capture for Chondrichthyans are virtually non-existent, jeopardizing the assessment of the real consequences of this practice and the development of effective fisheries management measures. We investigated whether trawling in semi-captive conditions impairs the reproductive success of pregnant Trygonorrhina dumerilii, a viviparous ray commonly caught as bycatch in southern Australian recreational and commercial fisheries. To do this we collected data on the occurrence of stillborn neonates, parturition timing, and neonates' dimension at birth, growth rate and performance (boldness, reflex, swimming and burying ability). Results highlighted that neonates born from mothers subjected to trawling simulation not only have a significantly lower body mass at birth, as recorded in a previous experiment, but also have a different allocation of yolk reserves and a lower growth rate, respond differently in the burying test, and swim for shorter distances when a predator attack is simulated. Smaller size and lower growth rate might expose neonates to a higher rate of predation, and similarly, the altered burying and swimming behaviour may be associated with a lower ability to escape from a predator. Further investigation is needed, but these first data suggest a possible reduction in neonates' survival rate and parents' fitness that can ultimately have severe repercussions on recruitment and population abundance in affected species.

abstract_text: The fossil record of modern sharks mainly consists of isolated teeth due to their poorly mineralized cartilaginous endoskeleton and a continuous tooth replacement that forms thousands of teeth during a sharks' lifetime. As a result, phylogenetic analyses of extinct shark taxa are mostly based on isolated teeth and therefore often lead to ambiguous results. The great white shark Carcharodon carcharias is known since the late Miocene, a period in which a number of big lamniform sharks occurred, i.e., †Otodus megalodon, †Cosmopolitodus hastalis and †Carcharodon hubbelli, which vanished after the Plio-Pleistocene marine megafauna extinction (2.5 mya). The evolutionary history of the great white shark remains highly debated and two hypotheses have been proposed: (1) C. carcharias is closely related to the megatoothed sharks, including †O. megalodon; (2) C. carcharias shares a more recent common ancestor with mako sharks and descended from the broad toothed mako shark †C. hastalis. Although the latter hypothesis is currently favoured, the occurrence of a narrow- and a broad-toothed form of †C. hastalis further complicates the reconstruction of the evolutionary history of the great white shark. Here we report of an exceptional find of two well preserved shark skeletons of a juvenile (TL ~1.7m) and an adult (TL ~5m) †Cosmopolitodus hastalis from the late Miocene Pisco Formation of Peru, which display broad teeth. The presence of articulated jaws allowed us to reconstruct the tooth files of this species and thus a more accurate phylogenetic analysis of lamniform sharks based on dental characters could be performed, including extinct mako sharks, Isurus spp. Furthermore, geometric morphometric analyses are performed to visualize the morphospace occupation of Isurus, †Cosmopolitodus and Carcharodon. This combined approach allowed us to reconstruct the origin of Carcharodon carcharias and the dental transition from fossil mako sharks to the extant great white shark.

abstract_text: Sharks are the marine top predators responsible for regulating population of other tertiary and quarternary consumers (i.e. fishes, seals and dolphins) and maintaining a naturally balanced trophic chain in the marine ecosystem. However, there is limited understanding on how these marine top predators are ecologically and biologically adapted to consume and digest such a wide variety of prey items, without hampering functional traits of the gastro-intestinal tract. Gastro-intestinal microbial community of sharks plays important different biological roles including development of vertebrae in juveniles, metabolising a wide variety of complex biomolecules, nutrient absorption and immune system response. Hammerhead sharks are characterised by intraspecific ontogenetic and sex partitioning of resources (i.e. habitat and diet) as reflected by satellite tagging, genetics and stable isotope analyses. However, it's unknown how gut microbial biota changes between juvenile and adult sharks (ontogenetic partitioning of resources) and also between female and male individuals (sex partitioning of resources) within species. This study analysed gut microbial community structure and composition of two Sphyrna spp. based on 16S rRNA gene tag sequencing at both intraspecific and interspecific levels. DNA was extracted using Zymobiomics DNA miniprep kit and sequences generated using paired-end sequencing on the Illumina MiSeq platform following the manufacturer's instructions. Quantitative Insights into Microbial Ecology (QIIME) analyses revealed non-significant changes in microbial community structure between juvenile and adult individuals and also between sexes within each species. The core microbiota included Actinobacteria, Flavobacteria, Protobacteria and Firmicutes whereas Proteobacteria were the most abundant phylum. This suggests gut microbiome of hammerhead sharks may be shaped by broader biological factors such as the host genotype and ambient environmental conditions rather than diet.

abstract_text: Our oceans are facing tremendous human-induced changes, including warming. As the temperature has increased, sudden warming events designated as marine heatwaves have become longer and more frequent with significant implications over marine ecosystems. As a crucial element of the marine environment, sharks may also be affected by these environmental changes. Exposure to ocean warming has shown to impact shark's predatory behavior, metabolism and overall fitness. However, the effects that a marine heatwave may have on these animals' physiology has not been addressed previously. Thus, the focus of our study was to investigate the impact of a marine heatwave (Δ3 °C) on the heamatological and respiratory systems of a juvenile temperate shark (Scyliorhinus canicula). To address this question, sharks were exposed to two treatments: control (18 °C) and category II marine heatwave (21 °C) for 15 days. We then analyzed the i) normal blood cell counts (e.g. erythrocytes, leucocytes and thrombocytes), ii) type and amount of EMNAs (erythrocyte nuclear morphological abnormalities), iii) spleen and heart to body ratios and iv) ventilation rates (before, initially and during the heatwave). According to our study, exposure to a category II marine heatwave drastically changed normal blood cell counts and ventilation rates. More specifically, the number of erythrocyte cells decreased, while the number of leukocyte and thrombocyte cells increased. Moreover, the amount of ventilation also increased. These findings may evidence that, during a sudden warming event, shark's ability to transport oxygen in red blood cells, linked to their need to ventilate more, might be significantly impaired. Furthermore, an increase of leukocytes and thrombocytes may explain the vulnerability and stress related to the increased temperature. As marine heatwaves are expected to aggravate with anthropogenic climate change, there is an urgency that should eager us to manage and mitigate its impacts.

abstract_text: Monitoring trends in shark body size and weight is fundamental for understanding their life history traits and elucidating population dynamics. Traditionally, size and weight information is acquired through invasive techniques, involving capture and handling. These protocols may undermine conservation efforts by causing physical damage, behavioral alterations, premature birth and even the death of the captured animals. This study tested the effectiveness of laser photogrammetry as a non-invasive technique for measuring morphometrics from five shark species housed in aquariums. The measured morphometrics were examined in regression analyses to provide a comprehensive set of lineal relationships for the estimation of shark total length and weight. The results obtained indicate that (1) this approach is effort and cost-effective; (2) laser metrics are highly precise, which ensures the reliability of the gathered morphometric information; and (3) accurate total length and weight estimates can be obtained from short morphometrics. These insights indicate that laser photogrammetry is a useful technique for assessing growth and life history parameters from free-swimming sharks. Therefore, this technique may constitute a valuable tool for aquariums to monitor sharks' health status and determine food requirements and medication doses. Furthermore, it has the potential to provide useful insights when applied to monitor sharks in their natural environments in order to implement effective management strategies. The compiled also models ease the obtention of total length and weight data, providing a long-needed resource in shark monitoring programs.

abstract_text: Sharks play both essential and diverse functional roles in marine ecosystems, having a remarkably long and successful evolutionary history. However, overfishing and habitat degradation, amidst other challenges, have ensued a steep population decline over the past decades. As CO2 emissions continue to increase, ocean acidification (OA) may come to pose an additional challenge to this group. In the present study, we investigated the potential impacts of OA-conditions (pCO2 ~900 µatm | Δ -0.3 pH units) over the embryonic development and juvenile metabolic physiology of a temperate shark, Scyliorhinus canicula. Aiming to evaluate the consequences of early exposure to high CO2 conditions, newly laid eggs were reared in either control or OA-treatment and, once hatched, individuals incubated under high CO2 were redistributed between both treatments. Both embryonic development, namely embryogenesis duration, hatching success, embryo activity, growth rate, body ratios, and juvenile metabolism, specifically their food intake, routine metabolic rate, maximum metabolic rate and aerobic scope, were evaluated. Overall, there were no significant changes in neither their development nor their metabolic physiology, regardless of early exposure to high CO2 levels. While this study highlights the coping capacity of sharks towards ocean acidification, the multiple and unpreceded pressures placed upon this group have the potential to undermine their inherent resilience. Hence, further research regarding different aspects of their biology and the numerous threats of the near-future is necessary to fully understand how this group may fare in the oceans of tomorrow.

abstract_text: Serum biochemistry and hematology profile are used to assess the physiological status of animal individuals and populations. Therefore, establishing reference intervals for serum biochemical and hematological analytes for wild populations of marine keystone species is important for their conservation. However, no such intervals have been established to date for many species in the Eastern Mediterranean, including the dusky shark (Carcharhinus obscurus) and sandbar shark (Carcharhinus plumbeus). In the Mediterranean, C. obscurus and C. plumbeus are classed as data deficient and endangered species, respectively, according to the IUCN Red List. This study aims to establish reference intervals for serum biochemical and hematological analytes in these two species. Blood samples have been collected from wild dusky and sandbar sharks captured during the tagging seasons that Morris Kahn Marine Research Station has been conducting since 2016. In the winters of 2016 and 2017, blood samples were obtained from 14 C. obscurus and 7 C. plumbeus individuals. This ongoing study has and will further expand this database during the winters of 2018 and 2019. To this point, serum samples of 19 C. obscurus (18 females and one male) and 12 C. plumbeus (all males) individuals were analyzed by spectrophotometry using an autoanalyzer, including 15 analytes: urea, total proteins, total bilirubin, glucose, cholesterol, triglycerides, inorganic phosphorus, chloride, sodium, potassium, total calcium, aspartate aminotransferase (AST), gamma-glutamyl transpeptidase (GGT), amylase, and creatine kinase (CK). For nine animals (four C. obscurus and five C. plumbeus), packed cell volume has been measured by centrifugation of heparinized capillaries, and manual leukocyte counts on blood smears have been done by microscopy. Preliminary results of serum biochemistry of both species are mostly consistent with findings of previous studies describing C. plumbeus in the Western Atlantic and other shark species in different locations. However, several analytes showed different values than previously described.

abstract_text: Chondrichthyes (sharks, rays and chimaeras) are the most basal jawed vertebrate lineage possessing the basic features of the human innate and adaptive immune systems, and thus are a key taxon to understand the emergence and evolution of vertebrate adaptive immunity. However, the few studies conducted to date have not provided a clear picture of the complexity of the genes involved in adaptive immunity in this oldest extant vertebrate class. Our results show that for the major histocompatibility complex (MHC) class I genes, involved in antigen presentation to T cells and Nature Killer (NK) cells, there is indeed a very high diversity in genetic lineages and copy number variation across taxa, at least as complex as has been found in mammals. abstract_text: In Israel, dusky and sandbar sharks (genus Carcharhinus) aggregate every winter at the warm water discharge of coastal power plants. This over wintering pattern is likely thermoregulatory in nature. Sightings of these species are increasingly rare in the Mediterranean, where shark populations have declined by 95% over the last decades. Sharks were tracked by acoustic telemetry, which enables detecting acoustic transmitters ('tags') by fixed underwater receivers. Since 2015, 17 sharks have been caught, measured and tagged in Hadera's hot waters, using acoustic tags and satellite tags. Acoustic tags are inserted into the shark's abdominal cavity, and satellite tags were attached to the dorsal fins. Both acoustic and satellite transmitters also recorded depth, and water temperature. Sharks were detected at the site for a long period (66 days ± 33.3 SD), and remained in the hot discharge while sea temperature kept decreasing. Daily movement analysis show sandbar sharks remain close to the bottom during daytime and moved to shallower water at night, while dusky sharks occupied very shallow water at all times. Data retrieved from one satellite tag showed a sandbar shark maintained the daily depth movement throughout its journey in open water. Temperature analysis show sharks stay within the elevated temperature zone throughout the season, away from the ambient temperature, until they leave the area completely. While one theory maintains that these aggregations are related to the gestation period in females, the residency of both female and male sharks suggest both genders benefit from the warm water. It is possible, that sharks are changing migration to warmer areas with the warm water at the station. Large scale movement study is crucial to understand the migration routes of these species in the Mediterranean Sea, and the implications of this phenomenon on their movement.

abstract_text: The sandbar shark, Carcharhinus plumbeus is one of the biggest sharks inhabiting the Mediterranean. It is a cosmopolitan species and wellknown from Boncuk Cove in Mediterranean coast of Turkey. Primary nursery grounds, defined as areas where parturition occurs, of Boncuk Cove C. plumbeus population. The aim of study is to determine secondary reproduction and nursery area of sandbar shark from Yumurtalık Bight, Eastern Mediterranean Sea. On 24-27 July 2017, Sandbar shark specimens were accidentally caught at a depth of 7 to 9 m off the Yumurtalik Bight (36°44'44.39"N, 35°42'22.77"E) by a pelagic bluefish longline. A total of 8 specimens (4 females and 4 males) were transported to the laboratory on ice. Each fish was measured for total length to the nearest 0.1 cm, weight (W) was weighted to the nearest 0.1 g and sex was determined by the presence of claspers. Total lengths and weights of C. plumbeus specimens were 54.5-61.0 cm, 930 - 1484 g, for males and 49.6 - 62.4 cm, 918 - 1568 g, respectively for females. In shark species, the embryo is connected to the mother by an umbilical cord. The umbilical scars are still clearly visible on these newly born sharks. The open umbilical scar lengths were between 4.1 and 5.0 mm and they were used as an indicator. Thus, this study provides the records of neonate and juveniles sandbar shark from the Yumurtalik Bight. It was determined that Yumurtalik Bight can be the second reproduction and nursery area of the sandbar sharks in the Mediterranean after Boncuk Cove in Gokova Bay, Turkey.

abstract_text: This study aims to provide general information regarding the effect of environmental factors on the occurrence of white sharks during ecotourism in Guadalupe Island, Mexico. The white sharks presence and environmental conditions were registered each hour during August-November of 2012-2014 in Rada Norte Bay (RNB). Analyzed environmental factors included sea surface temperature (SST), wind direction and speed, tide, moon phase, cloud cover, and water visibility. Sighting records were used to describe the white shark's probability of occurrence in relation to environmental factors, geographical position, and hour. Generalized additive models were applied using the presence/absence of the sharks as response variable according to the following categories: 1) Immature males; 2) Mature males; 3) Immature females; 4) Mature females. A total of 6,266 sightings of white sharks was registered according to sexual maturity during 98 days at RNB. Median from these records was 59 sightings per day (S.E.=5.96), and 9.82 sightings per hour (S.E.=1.22), with no significant differences in the sightings per hour related to the year (H2,90=6.35; P = 0.04), as confirmed by Bonferroni test. Regarding the month, a higher number of sightings per hour were observed during August (H3,90=21.20; P < 0.01), with no significant differences between the following months. The model for mature males suggests that there is a higher occurrence in the south part of RNB when SST is lower than 21°C, after new moon, and at any hour. In contrast, immature males' occurrence was higher in the west, during warm SST > 22°C, after full moon nights, and in the morning hours. Regarding females, mature individuals showed a higher probability of occurrence in the east, during warm SST > 23° C, early morning, and the last hours of the day. Explanations for these results will be discussed toward a potential segregation of white sharks in Guadalupe Island.

abstract_text: Spatiotemporal variation of the deposition of skate's eggcases on beaches of the french metropolitan coast from 2005 to 2017 was studied. Due to the lack of knowledge on skates nowadays, we hypothesized that eggcases' distribution can provide additional informations for fishery surveys and spatio-temporal variations. Data were provided by a citizen science program involving 1900 volunteers. The proximal goal of this project was to evaluate the influence of environmental factors, detect a long term evolution and define massive strand areas. A methodological challenge consisted in performing a reliable analysis on a large dataset (~465000 eggcases, 1077sites) based on opportunistic data where absence or sampling effort were not notified. Fortunately, we were able to mobilize a second dataset (~240000 eggcases, 30sites) which is more standardized allowing to investigate temporal autocorrelation. Furthermore for spatial analysis, we established a 5 km buffer from the coast to collect all types of habitat around. Eggcases of seven species were encountered, mostly Raja undulata, R.clavata and R.brachyura. Adequate analysis performed on the two dataset provided the same results within and between year variations. The evolution of egg's deposition within a year shows a neat phenology with a peak of increase during winter followed by a decrease during summer. Eggcase's deposition from undulate rays tend to increase significantly (26%) throughout the years. However, for other species it didn't show any inter-annuals significant trends. Undulate's eggs were mostly found near littoral rocks and coarse sands and tend not to be present near deep habitats while thornback's eggs can be found near both deep and tidal zones. They are qualified as opportunistic for habitats and depth according to literature and experts. Blonde ray's eggs were found near shallow zones in rocks and sandy bottoms. These results suggest that egg's deposition of skates over time can allow us to have more information on the biology and ecology of species.

abstract_text: Active acoustic surveys have been increasingly utilized as a non-extractive method for abundance estimation. These rely on species identification based on the focal animal's morphology, i.e., the dimensions of gas-filled structures such as the swim bladder, lungs, or other air cavities. Acoustic studies on elasmobranchs, which do not possess such structures, have dealt with the reflectivity of particularly large species or were unable to produce reliable size estimates, a prerequisite for density indexing. Furthermore, acoustic surveys typically employ narrow beam sonars which, with respect to highly-scattered populations, are mainly useful where animals are already known to occur as opposed to open-ocean waters. Thus, despite the potential usability of this method as the only non-extractive approach for real-time monitoring of deep-dwelling organisms, it remains limited to species of prominent acoustic features, as well as local-level surveys. We employed omni-directional transmitters to emit wideband acoustic signals and produce a time-delay image of continuously moving targets. The swimming trajectories of sharks and other species of apex predatory megafauna were compared with ground truth data to establish potential indicators to identify species irrespective of backscatter. Repetitions were performed in a variety of environmental settings throughout the Mediterranean marine space of Israel and included species that are listed as data deficient (DD), endangered (EN), and critically endangered (CR) in this region. Our findings provide for the non-extractive, fishery-independent sampling of highly-migratory megafauna across large spatial scales.

abstract_text: An Ecopath mass-balance model was applied to explore the ecological role of demersal sharks and rays (SR) distributed in the Calabrian sector of the North-Western Ionian Sea (Central Mediterranean Sea). Biomass data (ton/km2y) mostly derived from the standardized biomass index of demersal species in the time series of the EU MEDITS trawl survey. Landings (ton/km2y) and Discards (ton/km2y) data of commercial species collected from the time series EU Data Collection Framework, together with Production, Consumption and Diet data, were used to model the food web in its stationary state. A total of 58 functional groups (FGs) described the Calabrian food web over the 3469 km2 from Punta Alice to Cape Spartivento between 10-800 m of depth. The demersal SR species aggregated in the FG of the Shelf SR benthic feeders, the Shelf SR benthopelagic feeders, the Bathyal SR benthic feeders, the Bathyal sharks benthopelagic feeders and the Blackmouth catshark Galeus melastomus. Trophic levels (TL), Omnivory Index (OI), Keystoness Index (KSI), Mixed Trophic Impacts (MTI) and Exploitation rate (E) were estimated to describe their ecological traits. The highest and lowest TL were estimated for the Bathyal SR benthic feeders (Cetrophorus granulosus, Dipturus oxyrinchus) (4.94) and Bathyal sharks benthopelagic feeders (Etmopterus spinax, Dalatias licha, Chimaera monstrosa) (4.26). The OI indicated the Bathyal sharks benthopelagic feeders as more generalist than the other groups. Within this FG the Etmopterus spinax and D. licha are the more abundant keystone predators. The highest E rates were estimated for the G. melastomus (0.65) and Dasyatis pastinaca, Mustelus mustelus, Raja asterias included in the Shelf SR benthic feeders (0.57). Trawl impacted with the highest negative values of MTI on the Shelf SR benthic feeders (-0.599), the Bathyal sharks benthopelagic feeders (-0.404), the Shelf SR benthopelagic feeders (Raja miraletus, Scyliorhinus canicula and S. stellaris) (-0.324) and G. melastomus (-0.154).

abstract_text: A recent risk assessment for chondrichthyans (sharks, rays, and chimaeras) found some deepwater sharks were at relatively high risk of adverse impacts from fishing. Quantitative data for these species is limited, and some available information has been found to be unreliable. With a better understanding of spatial distributions, our knowledge of the risk to, and the status of these species would be more informed. This information would allow for the evaluation of potential stock boundaries, encourage comparisons of regional population structures, and overall, better inform fisheries management. abstract_text: The Western Central Atlantic (WCA) hosts a population of manta rays whose distribution and habitat preference is poorly understood to date. Obtaining this kind of information is crucial for effective conservation planning and implementation. In this study, we use ensemble ecological niche modelling (EENM) to predict the distribution of two sympatric manta ray species (Manta birostris and M. sp. cf birostris) in the WCA, and calculate the proportion of predicted suitable habitat that lies within protected areas. This technique has not been used to study the spatial ecology of manta rays at this scale before, but could prove to be a powerful tool in conservation planning. The EENM was developed combining 5,000 occurrence records derived from satellite tracking, diver observations, and verifiable social media posts. The predictions of the model indicate that suitable habitat for manta rays should be situated near the coast, in shallow and relatively warmer waters, especially near chlorophyll-α fronts. In the study region, key predicted suitable areas occur along the coasts of USA, Mexico, Nicaragua and Venezuela. Only 34% of predicted suitable habitat is encompassed by the present network of marine protected areas (MPAs), with just 0.2% in areas completely closed to fishing activities. The conservative life of oceanic manta rays makes this species sensitive to even moderate increases in mortality rates; for this reason, the existing MPAs may be likely to offer them little protection. As manta rays in the WCA are likely isolated from other populations worldwide, recolonization of the area following local extinction would be extremely unlikely and could even result in the loss of the endemic M. sp. cf birostris. Future conservation planning in the region should explicitly include conservation of manta rays in its targets, with particular focus on areas identified as key habitats for these species co-occurring in the WCA.

abstract_text: A unique stronghold for the Critically Endangered Angelshark (Squatina squatina) is found in the Canary Islands, where the species is still frequently encountered by divers and fishers. This provides a great opportunity to conduct research into Angelshark ecology, as limited understanding of Angelshark habitat use, movement and site fidelity at is a major factor preventing effective species protection and conservation. A key focus for Angel Shark Project: Canary Islands (ASP:CI) (a collaborative initiative between Universidad de Las Palmas de Gran Canaria, Zoological Research Museum Alexander Koenig and Zoological Society of London) is the investigation of juvenile Angelshark habitat in the region and identification of Angelshark nursery areas. The definition of shark nursery areas varies greatly in scientific literature, but ASP:CI have developed a multidisciplinary approach (using citizen science sightings, satellite imagery, focal surveys and mark-recapture techniques) to test the three nursery area criteria outlined in Heupel et al. 2007. Research over the last four years has identified that juvenile Angelsharks are present across a number of shallow, sheltered beaches in the Canary Islands. The team have identified two confirmed nursery areas, 13 potential nursery areas and 21 beaches where juvenile Angelsharks are observed. Mark-recapture work at the largest confirmed nursery area, Playa de Las Teresitas in Tenerife, confirms that juvenile Angelsharks remain present for up to 15 months. Data were used to develop a Guidance Document on the identification and protection of juvenile Angelshark habitat in the Canary Islands, which identifies eight key recommendations to improve protection of these areas.

abstract_text: Labial cartilages are paired structures located outside the jaws whose purpose in sharks is not completely clear yet. Labial cartilages vary a lot in current shark species, ranging from three pairs to a complete reduction, from massive to slender and from long to short. In our current work we used CT-images as a non-invasive method to check for labial cartilages in different shark species occupying different ecological niches and using different feeding strategies. The goal is to find out if the labial cartilages are a phylogenetic or an ecological trait. Therefore, we used nine species, which then were grouped according to their ecological niche into deep living, oceanic and benthic. We were able to detect that the labial cartilages in the oceanic species – especially in those known for ram-feeding behavior – were massively reduced while the ones in the benthic species were well conserved and strongly developed. Among the species classified by us as deep living we saw rather unique adaptations in the labial cartilages in comparison to the benthic group. For example, the cookie-cutter shark Isistius brasiliensis has very strong, fused labial cartilages and the ones of the frilled shark Chlamydoselachus anguineus are very slender. Therefore, we assume that the labial cartilages are an ecological trait and can give additional information on the feeding behavior in sharks and are also capable of giving information about the feeding behavior in extinct species, since labial cartilages were also detected in fossils. In future works we are going to check on as many species as possible to either confirm or refuse this theory. A phylogenetic signal was not discovered so far and the developmental basis of these structures still is ambiguous.

abstract_text: Coastal top predators are exposed to a wide variety of nutrient and contaminant sources due to the diversity of trophic chains within coastal areas. Here we measured mercury (Hg) isotopes in two co-occurring shark species (the bull shark Carcharhinus leucas and the tiger shark Galeocerdo cuvier) and their prey from a coastal ecosystem of the Indian Ocean, to (i) determine the main Hg source for these marine predators and (ii) explore the relevance of mercury isotopes as tracers of diet composition and feeding habitat. As Hg is mainly found under the methylmercury form in shark and teleost fish muscle, Hg isotope signatures (Δ199Hg and δ202Hg) of shark prey suggested that bull sharks were exposed to methylmercury produced in the water column while tiger sharks were exposed to mesopelagic methylmercury with additional microbial transformation in shelf sediments. Δ199Hg values efficiently traced the ecology of the two predators, demonstrating that bull sharks targeted coastal prey in shallow waters while tiger sharks were mainly foraging on shelf species in deeper waters. Unexpectedly, we found a large positive shift in δ202Hg between sharks and their prey, leading to high δ202Hg values in the two shark species. The shift in δ202Hg strongly suggests that significant Hg demethylation occurs in sharks, representing a protective mechanism to limit the accumulation of methylmercury and its toxic effects.

abstract_text: Global abundance of blue shark (Prionace glauca, L. 1758) has dramatically declined over the last 30 years, which is why, in some areas, this species has been categorized as "Critically Endangered" by the IUCN. Conservation and management of Mediterranean blue sharks (BS) suffer from a lack of knowledge regarding population structure and the dynamics of connectivity with contingents in the adjacent North-eastern Atlantic. Here, we filled in this knowledge gap by measuring genetic diversity and differentiation of BS individuals (N = 291) sampled across the Mediterranean Sea, and along the Atlantic continental slope of South- and North-western Europe, based on thousands of novel single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) developed through double-digest Restriction-site Amplified DNA (ddRAD) sequencing. SNP variation revealed a lack of genetic differences between Western and Eastern Mediterranean, and Mediterranean and North East Atlantic blue sharks, indicating the occurrence of a near- or full-panmixia across the North-eastern Atlantic and the Mediterranean. Therefore, the Mediterranean BS population can be considered an extension of the North-eastern Atlantic population, which is in contrast with the current stock delineation and management. These results are in contrast also with long term tagging data, which suggest that the blue shark don't cross the Strait of Gibraltar. These contrasting results highlight the need to integrate multidisciplinary studies to better reveals the connectivity of higly mobile species, such as the blue shark, in order to take more appropriate conservation actions. Beyond the region's population structure, we envision that the developed SNPs could be exploited for the traceability of BS products globally (e.g. Atlantic vs Pacific), helping to tackle the major threat to BS populations, represented by the millions of unreported by-caught blue sharks, which enter the global fin trade each year.

abstract_text: Cartilaginous fish represent less than 5% of marine fish species and in the Mediterranean Sea there are at least 79 species (45 shark species and 34 ray). Some sharks are considered apex predators and most of them are asynchronous opportunistic feeders. Predators play central role in marine and terrestrial environment. They exercise top-down control on lower trophic levels and compete one each other for same resources. Occasionally, opportunistic apex predators can attack another large predator (i.e. space competition). The Strait of Messina (central Mediterranean Sea) is a biodiversity hotspot thanks to its unique hydrodynamic regimes and host different shark species. In the last decade, several shark attacks over other predators in the Strait of Messina were documented between mainly in July. The attacked species were primarily swordfish (Xiphias gladius) but natural predation on giant devil ray (Mobula mobular) was also recorded. Generally, photos and video were taken after the harpooned swordfish were brought on board and are the only witness of these events. Indeed, most of the event stated here did happen after the animals were harpooned by feluca boats while swordfish (or other animals) were dead or life-fighting. These events were characterized by a well visible bite and removal of large muscle. The cause of the attacks most likely are associated to the weakness of the prey and the smell of blood and hormones released by injured fish. Since different species of shark inhabit the Strait of Messina, it is not really easy to identify shark species from the shape of the bite. There is also a lack of information and identification accuracy in species that inhabit or migrate through the Strait of Messina and therefore more research is needed to identify and monitor those highly mobile species and also to improve the knowledge on its behaviour.

abstract_text: Pelagic sharks include oceanic and semi-oceanic species, and are mostly represented by the orders Carcharhiniformes, Lamniformes, and Squaliformes. Due to their complex life cycle, research on these organisms can be difficult in terms of logistic and finance. Because of this, the use of touristic operations and citizen science has been seen as an effective method to study these animals in areas where their abundance is significant. Due to the characteristics of the study area, we expect to find a high species richness, as well as seasonal patterns regarding relative abundance of sharks as a function of environmental factors. The main goal of this study was to create an inventory of pelagic shark species in Cabo San Lucas, and identify seasonal patterns in their abundance, as well as contribute data that supports the use of tourism on the study of pelagic species. To do this, submarine censuses were completed, registering shark species' richness, relative abundance, sex and size of the individuals, as well as environmental factors such as sea surface temperature, wind speed, cloudiness and depth (if possible). We observed 8 species during the censuses, with the most abundant being Carcharhinus falciformis, Sphyrna zygaena, and Isurus oxyrinchus. Also, we identified seasonal patterns on the relative abundance of the latter, where I. oxyrinchus was the most dominant species during the cold season (December-March), S. zygaena during the transitional period (April-June), and C. falciformis during the warm season (July-November). This is the first formal inventory of species done for the area, and we were able to demonstrate the viability of touristic operations and citizen science as tools used for the constant monitoring of these organisms and the establishment of baselines for these populations. This is especially important since these species are being taken advantage of by the growing nature tourism sector in Mexico.

title: Of Shark and Men: Data sourced from ecotourism to study the impact of environmental conditions on great white shark behaviour

abstract_text: Difficulties in sampling large, mobile marine predators, such as great white sharks (Carcharodon carcharias) have hindered the investigation of behaviour, but collaboration with ecotourism companies could offer an alternative data resource for scientific research. White Shark Africa (of Mossel Bay South Africa) volunteered data collected by their onboard crew during tourist excursions from 2009 through 2011, constituting of over 660 sampling hours and 985 individual shark sightings. The behaviour observed during each trip was used to assign each shark sighting to a 'behavioural state' (to encompass the overall behaviour of the shark on that trip), termed 'aggressive', 'cautious' and 'inquisitive'. Multiple explanatory variables related to weather, environment, seasonality, anthropic activity, conspecific presence and individual demographics were subjected to generalised linear models to identify variables which were significantly related to the presence of each behavioural state. Classification trees were used to analyse how significant variables affected white shark behaviours. Cautious behavioural state was found to be related to the order in which sharks arrived at the boat, the size of the shark and the bait type used. The probability of observing cautious behaviour was highest for sharks of smaller size (TL) which were first to arrive at the boat, and when baiting with tuna and snoek. Comparatively, aggressive behavioural state, was found to be related to running average minimum air temperatures (RTMIN) and arrival time. The probability of observing aggressive behaviour was highest during early morning sampling and when the RTMIN was low. Inquisitive behavioural state was also found to be significantly related to arrival time, but also to sea surface temperature (SST). The probability of observing inquistive behaviours was also highest during early morning sampling, but also when SST was warmer. Overall, modelling indicated that environmental conditions, anthropic activity, shark size and the presence of conspecifics all impacted on white shark behaviour. This study was the first to use ecotourism data in ethological research and the results indicate that collaboration with ecotourism operators could be invaluable for the collection of large, high-power data sets. Data sourced from ecotourism could be used in a wide array of scientific studies, as long as rigorous statistical methods are applied, and the results interpreted with consideration of the sampling methodology.

abstract_text: The Top Predator laboratory of Morris Kahn Marine Research Station has been running a shark-tagging project in the last 4 years, as part of a long-term ecological research programme. The study takes place at an anthropogenic, seasonal aggregation area of sharks in the warm discharge waters of power plants along the Mediterranean coast of Israel. Following the tagging protocol of Sharklab (Bimini, Bahamas), 51 sharks have been tagged thus far, of which 35 were dusky sharks (Carcharhimus obscurus; 34 females and 1 male) and 16 sandbar sharks (Carcharhinus plumbeus; all male). These species are listed by the IUCN as data deficient (DD) and endangered (EN) in the Mediterranean Sea, respectively. The tagging procedure includes morphometric measurements as well as DNA, stable isotopes, blood chemistry and microbiome sampling. All tagged sharks are issued a subcutaneous PIT tag as well as a spaghetti tag. 19 dusky sharks and 10 sandbar sharks were tagged with acoustic transmitters and an array of 11 receivers was placed within the tagging site and in other aggregation areas, such as offshore mariculture facilities, throughout Israel's marine space. Results indicate thermo-regulated fidelity at human-altered habitats and size as well as sex-dependent aggregating behaviour. In the Mediterranean Sea, where shark populations have declined dramatically over the last 70 years, Israeli waters have become an oasis for coastal sharks and a hub for their research, supported by ground-breaking conservation, legislation and enforcement.

title: Emerging Technologies in Acoustic Telemetry: Real-time vs. Data Storage

abstract_text: Acoustic telemetry is a well-established tool that has been used around the world for more than three decades to get an understanding of the spatio-temporal movements and associated behaviour of a wide range of aquatic animals. New emerging technologies are being developed continuously that allow for new research applications and designs. Examples for these new technologies are (1) real-time observations of both aquatic animals as well as their aquatic environment and (2) acoustic data storage tags. Applied real-time systems may consist of various underwater sensors, acoustic telemetry tags on aquatic animals, a surface hub that receives data from the sensors as well as from the tags, and a cloud-centric database. Such systems are now in use at several global installations. Data access is available via a mobile phone or laptop that provide real-time notifications when tagged animals are near receivers or the current state of environmental variables. Acoustic data storage tags might be used especially for far-ranging animals such as sharks and rays that might inhabit coastal and pelagic regions at different times of the year. These applications can be used to get a bigger picture of a species behaviour and its spatio-temporal distribution in order to address conservation and management measures since data is also collected while animals are outside of acoustic arrays. Here, we will explore the evolution of the use of acoustic telemetry and how receiving data in real-time and in acoustic data storage applications will help sustain our ocean ecosystems.

abstract_text: Information like habitat preferences and trophic ecology regarding juvenile white sharks Carcharodon carcharias (WS) and shortfin mako sharks Isurus oxyrinchus (MS) is lacking. This study investigates the habitat use of juvenile MS and WS in the nursery area of Sebastian Vizcaino Bay (SVB) using stable isotope analysis in multiple tissues. During 2015 and 2016, we collected muscle (n=165), blood samples (n=147), red blood cells (RBC; n=62) and plasma (n=70) of young MS and muscle (n=6), RBC (=2) and plasma (n=2) of young WS. The size range for MS was 64.5-196 cm of total length (TL) and for WS it was 130-292 cm TL. Shortfin mako and white sharks had significant differences for muscle tissue in δ13C values (W = 255.5, p < 0.0001), but not in δ15N values (W = 1189.5, p = 0.08). We did not find significant differences in δ13C values (W = 228, p-value = 0.045) and δ15N values (W = 420.5, p-value = 0.8) of whole blood between shortfin mako and white sharks. In addition, sharks with similar TL of both species (MS > 102 cm TL and WS <186 cm TL) showed a similar pattern of δ15N values for whole blood, RBCs and plasma. MS and WS with similar total length (MS> 102 cm TL and WS < 186 cm TL) reflected in their tissues (muscle, blood, RBC and plasma) the regional baseline 15-N enriched isotopic signature of SVB, suggesting that SVB has a unique isotopic signature (isoscape). The similarity in isotopic niche and isotopic composition between shortfin mako and white sharks in multiple tissues reflecting large and short time periods suggest shared resource and common habitat use inside SVB throughout extended times confirming their residency in this area during their earlier life stages.

abstract_text: Whale sharks are usually observed in coastal areas throughout the highly productive tropical and subtropical regions. The Indo-Pacific sub-population is declining mainly due to fisheries catches, bycatch and vessel strikes. Accordingly, in 2016 the species was assessed as "Endangered" on the IUCN Red List. Despite conservation concerns, there are still substantial gaps in the knowledge of whale shark ecology. This study investigates the temporal variability of whale shark presence in the South Ari Atoll Marine Protected Area (S.A.MPA). Even if the area is very limited (about 42km2) it appears to be an important aggregation site for the species in the Maldives archipelago. Since 2012 the Maldives Whale Shark Research Programme (MWSRP) has been collecting data year-round within the MPA. Due to the heterogeneity of the effort among different years only data collected between 2014 and 2017 has been considered in this study. A total of 572 sharks encounters have been reported in this period. Concurrently, in situ Sea Surface Temperature (SST) has also been collected. Sightings per Unit of Effort (SPUE) was calculated based on the number of survey trips carried out per month and per year during favorable environmental conditions (e.g. wind speed not exceed 3 in the Beaufort scale and partial and total clouds covered conditions). Generalized Linear Models have been used to analyse the temporal variability of the SPUE. No significant difference has been observed in SPUE across the study period. However, taking into consideration data on a monthly-year basis, the species' occurrence presents significant differences (P-level < 0.01). Further analysis revealed that SST could be a significant covariate. The understanding offered by this study provides additional information upon which to base an appropriate management strategy in the MPA for this wide-ranging species.

abstract_text: The North Sea is known for its natural richness. Yet it is also one of most intensively exploited seas in the world, and, as a result, fish species have disappeared or populations are reduced to low numbers. There is a growing call to restore the natural richness of the North Sea but, it is often unclear what this is, because baseline studies date back 60 years at best. Elasmobranchs are an example of a group of species of which populations in the North Sea have marginalized over the past century. These includes the critically endangered angelshark Squatina squatina and common skate Dipturus intermedius. We review the historical abundance and some life-history aspects of these species in the Dutch marine waters using a variety of historical sources. Palaeontological sources dating back to the origin of the North Sea suggest that these species always have been present in the area. Written historical sources from the 16th to the 19th century suggest that the angelshark used to be fairly common and that the common skate was indeed common. Catch reports indicate that the angel shark started to decline at the onset of the 20th century and went locally extinct in the 1970s. Landings and fishery-independent data of common skate show a similar picture. The start of the decline coincides with the onset of steam-powered fisheries whereas the demise follows on the intensification of diesel-powered beam-trawlers. Historical reports and catch data indicates that angelsharks mainly visited the area in summer to reproduce. Common skates were mainly caught in winter and these were mostly young individuals that supposedly used the area as nursery grounds. Our study shows that if we base our ideas of a North Sea ecosystem on a baseline view after 1900 we may have overly low expectations of its potential natural richness.
